items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "pulmonary circulation"?
options: A system of blood vessels with a pump and valves to ensure one-way flow of blood.
The circuit that carries blood between the heart and the lungs.
A system in which blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body.
The circuit that carries blood between the heart and the rest of the body.
items.answer: The circuit that carries blood between the heart and the lungs.
items.markingKey: Pulmonary circulation: the circuit that carries blood between the heart and the lungs.

items.stem: Explain the advantages of a double circulation in mammals.
items.answer: Blood returns to the heart after collecting oxygen in the lungs and is pumped again at high pressure, so oxygen is delivered quickly to respiring tissues; low pressure in lungs avoids damage to capillaries.
items.markingKey: high pressure to body [1]; fast oxygen delivery for high metabolic rate [1]; low pressure to lungs [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why fish can survive with a single circulation.
items.answer: Fish are supported by water and their body temperature is the same as the water, so they need less energy and oxygen than mammals; slower delivery is enough.
items.markingKey: lower energy / oxygen demand [1]; no need to maintain body temperature [1] [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which blood flows through them in the human double circulation: pulmonary artery, lungs, left atrium, pulmonary vein.
items.answer: pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium
items.markingKey: pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium (all correct [2]; one error [1]) [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which blood flows through them in the human double circulation: aorta, body organs, lungs, left ventricle, left atrium, pulmonary vein.
items.answer: lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body organs
items.markingKey: lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body organs (all correct [2]; one error [1]) [2]

items.stem: Blood pressure was measured in a fish: 30 mmHg leaving the heart and 12 mmHg after the gills. In a mammal, pressure leaving the left ventricle is 130 mmHg. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in blood pressure as blood passes through the gills. (b) Suggest why mammals need a higher blood pressure to their body than fish.
items.answer: (a) 60% (b) Mammals have high metabolic rates (maintaining body temperature) so need rapid delivery of oxygen and glucose to cells.
items.markingKey: (a) (30 − 12) ÷ 30 × 100 [1] = 60% [1] [2] (b) higher energy demand [1]; faster delivery [1] [2]

items.stem: In a fish, blood flows from the heart to the
options: body, then to the heart, then to the gills
lungs, then to the heart, then to the body
gills, then back to the heart, then to the body
gills, then to the body, then back to the heart
items.answer: gills, then to the body, then back to the heart
items.markingKey: Single circulation: heart → gills → body → heart.

items.stem: Explain why blood pressure is low after passing through the gills of a fish.
items.answer: Pressure is lost as blood is pushed through the narrow capillaries of the gills, and it is not re-pumped before going to the body.
items.markingKey: pressure lost in capillaries [1]; not re-pumped [1] [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which blood flows through them in the human double circulation: left ventricle, pulmonary vein, aorta, left atrium.
items.answer: pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta
items.markingKey: pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta (all correct [2]; one error [1]) [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which blood flows through them in the human double circulation: pulmonary vein, lungs, left atrium, body organs, aorta, left ventricle.
items.answer: lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body organs
items.markingKey: lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body organs (all correct [2]; one error [1]) [2]

items.stem: Blood pressure was measured in a fish: 35 mmHg leaving the heart and 12 mmHg after the gills. In a mammal, pressure leaving the left ventricle is 110 mmHg. (a) Explain why the pressure falls in the gills. (b) Explain how the double circulation of the mammal avoids this problem.
items.answer: (a) Friction / resistance in the narrow gill capillaries. (b) Blood returns to the heart from the lungs and is pumped again by the left ventricle at high pressure to the body.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) returns to heart [1]; re-pumped at high pressure [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "septum"?
options: A disease in which the coronary arteries become blocked by fatty deposits, reducing the supply of oxygen to heart muscle.
The wall of muscle that separates the left and right sides of the heart.
Arteries that supply the heart muscle with oxygen and glucose.
The number of times the heart beats per minute.
items.answer: The wall of muscle that separates the left and right sides of the heart.
items.markingKey: Septum: the wall of muscle that separates the left and right sides of the heart.

items.stem: Explain why heart rate increases during exercise.
items.answer: Muscles respire faster and need more oxygen and glucose and must remove more carbon dioxide; a faster heart rate pumps blood to them more quickly.
items.markingKey: more oxygen / glucose needed [1]; remove CO₂ [1]; faster delivery [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how a blocked coronary artery can cause a heart attack.
items.answer: Heart muscle beyond the blockage receives no oxygen or glucose, so it cannot respire aerobically and stops contracting or dies.
items.markingKey: no oxygen to heart muscle [1]; cannot respire / dies [1] [2]

items.stem: Grace measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 127, 101, 86, 81, 77, 74, 71; trial 2: 128, 99, 90, 78, 77, 75, 70; trial 3: 124, 145, 90, 82, 75, 74, 74. Calculate the mean pulse rate at 6 min, ignoring any anomalous result.
items.answer: 71.7 beats/min

items.stem: Noah measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 128, 102, 91, 82, 76, 72, 71; trial 2: 127, 104, 90, 49, 76, 73, 72; trial 3: 129, 105, 91, 81, 75, 72, 70. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) The pulse rate is highest immediately after exercise and then decreases, returning towards the resting rate after several minutes. (b) Use a pulse oximeter / heart rate monitor for accuracy.
items.markingKey: (a) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (b) Any one from: use a pulse oximeter / heart rate monitor for accuracy; use a metronome so every student steps at the same rate; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the time after exercise (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Sipho measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 136, 107, 54, 81, 76, 74, 72; trial 2: 131, 108, 91, 84, 77, 74, 74; trial 3: 136, 106, 89, 81, 75, 76, 71. items.answer: (a) Independent: time after exercise; dependent: pulse rate. (b) A line graph: time after exercise on the x-axis and mean pulse rate on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = time after exercise [1]; dependent variable = pulse rate [1] [2] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; time after exercise on x-axis and pulse rate on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Sofia measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 129, 106, 87, 83, 77, 72, 74; trial 2: 132, 106, 87, 83, 75, 74, 73; trial 3: 77, 104, 89, 79, 77, 76, 74. items.answer: (a) 130.5 beats/min (b) A line graph: time after exercise on the x-axis and mean pulse rate on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) (129 + 132) ÷ 2 [1] = 130.5 beats/min [1] [2] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; time after exercise on x-axis and pulse rate on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 126, 149, 89, 79, 76, 75, 73; trial 2: 128, 102, 88, 82, 77, 72, 71; trial 3: 128, 106, 89, 82, 74, 74, 73. (a) Calculate the mean pulse rate at 1 min, ignoring any anomalous result. (b) Describe the trend shown by the results. (c) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) 104 beats/min (b) The pulse rate is highest immediately after exercise and then decreases, returning towards the resting rate after several minutes. (c) Use a pulse oximeter / heart rate monitor for accuracy.
items.markingKey: (a) (102 + 106) ÷ 2 [1] = 104 beats/min [1] [2] (b) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (c) Any one from: use a pulse oximeter / heart rate monitor for accuracy; use a metronome so every student steps at the same rate; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the time after exercise (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "coronary heart disease"?
options: A lower, muscular chamber of the heart that pumps blood into arteries.
The number of times the heart beats per minute.
An upper chamber of the heart that receives blood from veins.
A disease in which the coronary arteries become blocked by fatty deposits, reducing the supply of oxygen to heart muscle.
items.answer: A disease in which the coronary arteries become blocked by fatty deposits, reducing the supply of oxygen to heart muscle.
items.markingKey: Coronary heart disease: a disease in which the coronary arteries become blocked by fatty deposits, reducing the supply of oxygen to heart muscle.

items.stem: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?
options: It pumps blood all round the body at higher pressure
It receives blood from the vena cava
It pumps blood to the lungs
items.answer: It pumps blood all round the body at higher pressure
items.markingKey: The right ventricle pumps only to the lungs (lower pressure).

items.stem: A student counts 20 pulse beats in 30 seconds. What is the heart rate?
items.answer: 40 beats/min

items.stem: Ravi counts 21 pulse beats in 20 seconds. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute.
items.answer: 63 beats/min

items.stem: Sipho counts 21 pulse beats in 20 seconds. Calculate the heart rate in beats per minute. Each beat pumps 75 cm³ of blood. Calculate the volume of blood pumped per minute (cardiac output) in dm³.
items.answer: 63 beats/min; 4.72 dm³/min

items.stem: Diego measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 131, 157, 90, 81, 76, 73, 73; trial 2: 130, 109, 89, 82, 77, 73, 74; trial 3: 132, 106, 90, 81, 75, 76, 72. (a) Calculate the mean pulse rate at 1 min, ignoring any anomalous result. (b) Describe the trend shown by the results. (c) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) 107.5 beats/min (b) The pulse rate is highest immediately after exercise and then decreases, returning towards the resting rate after several minutes. (c) A line graph: time after exercise on the x-axis and mean pulse rate on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) (109 + 106) ÷ 2 [1] = 107.5 beats/min [1] [2] (b) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (c) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; time after exercise on x-axis and pulse rate on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "the vein that carries blood from the gut to the liver"?
items.answer: Hepatic portal vein
items.markingKey: Hepatic portal vein: the vein that carries blood from the gut to the liver.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function.
items.answer: Thick muscular and elastic walls withstand high pressure and stretch and recoil with each heartbeat to maintain pressure; narrow lumen keeps pressure high.
items.markingKey: thick wall / high pressure [1]; elastic recoil [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how blood in the veins of the legs returns to the heart.
items.answer: Contraction of surrounding skeletal muscles squeezes the veins; valves prevent backflow, so blood is pushed towards the heart.
items.markingKey: muscles squeeze [1]; valves prevent backflow [1] [2]

items.stem: Which blood vessel has this structure: thick, elastic, muscular wall; narrow lumen?
items.answer: artery
items.markingKey: Artery: thick, elastic, muscular wall; narrow lumen; carries blood at high pressure away from the heart.

items.stem: Measurements of three blood vessels: vessel X: wall 1080 μm, lumen 2716 μm; vessel Y: wall 434 μm, lumen 7865 μm; vessel Z: wall 1 μm, lumen 8 μm. Identify each vessel and give a reason for each identification.
items.answer: X: artery; Y: vein; Z: capillary
items.markingKey: X artery [1]; Y vein [1]; Z capillary [1]; reasons: artery thick wall / narrow lumen, vein thinner wall / wide lumen, capillary wall one cell (about 1 μm) [2] [5]

items.stem: In a biology lesson in Cape Town, students examine prepared slides of an artery and a vein cut in cross-section, and a capillary network in a muscle. (a) Explain how the structure of capillaries is adapted for exchange. (b) Name the vessels that carry blood to and from the liver.
items.answer: (a) Walls one cell thick give short diffusion distance; many branches give large surface area; narrow lumen slows blood. (b) Hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein (to); hepatic vein (from).
items.markingKey: (a) two points [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why capillaries form dense networks in active tissues such as muscles.
items.answer: Every cell is close to a capillary, so the diffusion distance for oxygen and glucose is short and there is a large surface area for exchange.
items.markingKey: short distance [1]; large surface area [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the pressure of blood in veins is lower than in arteries.
items.answer: Pressure is lost as blood passes through narrow capillaries; veins are further from the heart.

items.stem: Blood pressure in the aorta is 120 mmHg, in the capillaries 32 mmHg and in the vena cava 5 mmHg. Calculate the percentage decrease in pressure between the aorta and the capillaries.

In a biology lesson in Cairo, students examine prepared slides of an artery and a vein cut in cross-section, and a capillary network in a muscle. (a) Describe two differences between the artery and the vein that the students would see. (b) Explain how the structure of capillaries is adapted for exchange.
items.answer: (a) Artery: thicker, muscular, elastic wall and narrower lumen; vein: thinner wall, wider lumen (may look flattened) and valves. (b) Walls one cell thick give short diffusion distance; many branches give large surface area; narrow lumen slows blood.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) two points [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "red blood cells"?
items.answer: Transport oxygen (haemoglobin).
items.markingKey: Red blood cells: transport oxygen (haemoglobin).

items.stem: Describe how a blood clot forms at a wound.
items.answer: Platelets at the wound release chemicals; soluble fibrinogen is converted to insoluble fibrin; fibrin forms a mesh that traps red blood cells, forming a clot that dries to a scab.
items.markingKey: platelets [1]; fibrinogen → fibrin [1]; mesh traps cells [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why people living at high altitude have more red blood cells.
items.answer: Air at altitude has less oxygen; more red blood cells (haemoglobin) allow enough oxygen to be carried to tissues.
items.markingKey: less oxygen at altitude [1]; more haemoglobin to carry oxygen [1] [2]

items.stem: Which component of blood has this function: help blood to clot?
items.answer: platelets
items.markingKey: Platelets: help blood to clot.

items.stem: State the function of each component of blood: (i) phagocytes, (ii) lymphocytes, (iii) plasma.
items.answer: (i) engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis) (ii) produce antibodies (iii) transports blood cells, ions, glucose, amino acids, hormones, CO₂, urea and plasma proteins
items.markingKey: (i) engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis) [1]; (ii) produce antibodies [1]; (iii) transports blood cells, ions, glucose, amino acids, hormones, CO₂, urea and plasma proteins [1] [3]

items.stem: Amara cuts a finger in the kitchen. Within a few minutes the bleeding stops and a scab forms. Two days later the area around the cut is red and swollen. (a) Suggest why the area became red and swollen. (b) Describe how two types of white blood cell would respond.
items.answer: (a) Pathogens entered; more blood flows to the area and white blood cells move in to destroy pathogens. (b) Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to the pathogen.
items.markingKey: (a) infection [1]; white blood cells / blood flow [1] [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain how phagocytes protect the body.
items.answer: They move towards pathogens, engulf them by phagocytosis and digest them with enzymes.
items.markingKey: engulf [1]; digest [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a person with very few platelets bruises and bleeds easily.
items.answer: Platelets are needed to start clotting; without enough, wounds do not seal quickly.

items.stem: A blood test shows 5.6 million red blood cells and 7,000 white blood cells per mm³. Calculate the ratio of red blood cells to white blood cells, to the nearest whole number.

Mohammed cuts a finger in the kitchen. Within a few minutes the bleeding stops and a scab forms. Two days later the area around the cut is red and swollen. (a) Explain why the clot is important besides preventing blood loss. (b) Suggest why the area became red and swollen. (c) Describe how two types of white blood cell would respond.
items.answer: (a) It forms a barrier to the entry of pathogens. (b) Pathogens entered; more blood flows to the area and white blood cells move in to destroy pathogens. (c) Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to the pathogen.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) infection [1]; white blood cells / blood flow [1] [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: What is an advantage of a double circulatory system?
options: The heart needs only one chamber
Blood flows through the gills twice
Blood is pumped at high pressure to the body after the lungs
items.answer: Blood is pumped at high pressure to the body after the lungs
items.markingKey: Blood returns to the heart after the lungs and is re-pressurised, so delivery to tissues is fast.

items.stem: Jonas says: "Fish have a double circulation because they have two gills." Explain whether Jonas is correct.
items.answer: Fish have a single circulation: blood passes through the heart once per circuit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Fish have a single circulation: blood passes through the heart once per circuit. [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which blood flows through them in the human double circulation: lungs, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, right ventricle.
items.answer: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein
items.markingKey: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein (all correct [2]; one error [1]) [2]

items.stem: Put these in the order in which blood flows through them in the human double circulation: pulmonary artery, right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary vein, left atrium, lungs.
items.answer: right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium
items.markingKey: right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium (all correct [2]; one error [1]) [2]

items.stem: Blood pressure was measured in a fish: 25 mmHg leaving the heart and 10 mmHg after the gills. In a mammal, pressure leaving the left ventricle is 110 mmHg. (c) Explain how the double circulation of the mammal avoids this problem.
items.answer: (a) 60% (b) Friction / resistance in the narrow gill capillaries. (c) Blood returns to the heart from the lungs and is pumped again by the left ventricle at high pressure to the body.

items.stem: What is the function of the valves in the heart?
options: To prevent the backflow of blood
items.answer: To prevent the backflow of blood
items.markingKey: Atrioventricular and semilunar valves keep flow one-way.

items.stem: Explain why the septum is important.
items.answer: It separates oxygenated blood in the left side from deoxygenated blood in the right side, so they do not mix and the body receives highly oxygenated blood.
items.markingKey: prevents mixing [1]; more oxygen delivered [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how stents and angioplasty treat coronary heart disease.
items.answer: A balloon is inflated in the narrowed artery to widen it (angioplasty) and a mesh tube (stent) is left in place to hold it open, restoring blood flow.
items.markingKey: balloon widens [1]; stent holds open [1] [2]

items.stem: Deaths from coronary heart disease per 100 000 men aged 45–64 in a study in Seoul: non-smokers: 99; light smokers: 203; heavy smokers: 292. (a) Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for heavy smokers than for non-smokers. (b) Explain how smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
items.answer: (a) 2.95 times (b) Chemicals in smoke (and nicotine) damage artery linings and raise blood pressure, encouraging fatty deposits in coronary arteries; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried.
items.markingKey: (a) 292 ÷ 99 = 2.95 [1] (b) damages artery walls / raises blood pressure [1]; fatty deposits block coronary arteries [1] [3]

items.answer: 72.7 beats/min

items.stem: A doctor in Singapore listens to a patient's heart and explains how the heart pumps blood through the double circulation. (a) Explain the function of the semilunar valves. (b) Explain why the ventricle walls are thicker than the atrium walls.
items.answer: (a) They stop blood flowing back from the arteries into the ventricles when the ventricles relax. (b) Ventricles pump blood out of the heart to the lungs or body (further, higher pressure); atria pump only into the ventricles.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "vein"?
options: The space inside a blood vessel through which blood flows.
A tiny blood vessel with a wall one cell thick where substances are exchanged with tissues.
The vein that carries blood from the gut to the liver.
A blood vessel with a thin wall, wide lumen and valves that carries blood back to the heart at low pressure.
items.answer: A blood vessel with a thin wall, wide lumen and valves that carries blood back to the heart at low pressure.
items.markingKey: Vein: a blood vessel with a thin wall, wide lumen and valves that carries blood back to the heart at low pressure.

items.stem: A student in Riyadh states: "Capillaries have thick walls to stop them bursting." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Capillary walls are one cell thick for fast diffusion; pressure in capillaries is lower than in arteries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Capillary walls are one cell thick for fast diffusion; pressure in capillaries is lower than in arteries. [2]

items.answer: Red blood cells carry oxygen; platelets help blood clot.

items.answer: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin; white blood cells defend against pathogens.

items.answer: Twice

items.answer: left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body organs

items.stem: Which is a risk factor for coronary heart disease?
items.answer: Smoking
items.markingKey: Risk factors: diet high in saturated fat, smoking, stress, lack of exercise, genetics, age, sex.

items.stem: Explain how regular exercise can reduce the risk of coronary heart disease.
items.answer: Exercise strengthens the heart muscle, helps reduce blood pressure, body mass and blood cholesterol, so fewer fatty deposits form in coronary arteries.
items.markingKey: lower cholesterol / mass / pressure [1]; less fatty deposit / blockage [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the atrioventricular valves work when the ventricles contract.
items.answer: Pressure in the ventricles rises above that in the atria, pushing the valves shut so blood cannot flow back into the atria; it is forced into the arteries.

items.stem: Deaths from coronary heart disease per 100 000 men aged 45–64 in a study in Cairo: non-smokers: 103; light smokers: 145; heavy smokers: 262. (a) Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for heavy smokers than for non-smokers. (b) Explain how smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
items.answer: (a) 2.54 times (b) Chemicals in smoke (and nicotine) damage artery linings and raise blood pressure, encouraging fatty deposits in coronary arteries; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried.
items.markingKey: (a) 262 ÷ 103 = 2.54 [1] (b) damages artery walls / raises blood pressure [1]; fatty deposits block coronary arteries [1] [3]

items.stem: Felix measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 140, 159, 93, 83, 77, 77, 73; trial 2: 138, 106, 93, 83, 78, 77, 72; trial 3: 134, 112, 91, 82, 78, 73, 71. Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it.
items.answer: Trial 1 at 1 min (159 beats/min); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated).
items.markingKey: trial 1 at 1 min identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2]

items.stem: Mateo measured the pulse rate of a group of students at rest and then every minute after 2 minutes of step-ups. Results table. Time after exercise / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Pulse rate / beats/min, trial 1: 122, 102, 88, 80, 73, 74, 71; trial 2: 119, 101, 85, 79, 45, 71, 71; trial 3: 125, 98, 85, 80, 73, 72, 71. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Calculate the percentage increase in pulse rate from the value at 6 minutes to the value immediately after exercise.
items.answer: (a) Trial 2 at 4 min (45 beats/min); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) 72%

items.stem: Which term is defined as "a blood vessel with a thick muscular, elastic wall that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure"?
items.answer: Artery
items.markingKey: Artery: a blood vessel with a thick muscular, elastic wall that carries blood away from the heart at high pressure.

items.stem: Samuel says: "Capillaries have thick walls to stop them bursting." Explain whether Samuel is correct.
items.answer: Capillary walls are one cell thick for fast diffusion; pressure in capillaries is lower than in arteries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Capillary walls are one cell thick for fast diffusion; pressure in capillaries is lower than in arteries. [2]

In a biology lesson in Accra, students examine prepared slides of an artery and a vein cut in cross-section, and a capillary network in a muscle. (a) Describe two differences between the artery and the vein that the students would see. (b) Explain how the structure of capillaries is adapted for exchange. (c) Name the vessels that carry blood to and from the liver.
items.answer: (a) Artery: thicker, muscular, elastic wall and narrower lumen; vein: thinner wall, wider lumen (may look flattened) and valves. (b) Walls one cell thick give short diffusion distance; many branches give large surface area; narrow lumen slows blood. (c) Hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein (to); hepatic vein (from).
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) two points [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: A student in Doha states: "White blood cells contain haemoglobin." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Red blood cells contain haemoglobin; white blood cells defend against pathogens.

items.stem: A blood test shows 5.6 million red blood cells and 9,000 white blood cells per mm³. Calculate the ratio of red blood cells to white blood cells, to the nearest whole number.

Kenji cuts a finger in the kitchen. Within a few minutes the bleeding stops and a scab forms. Two days later the area around the cut is red and swollen. (a) Describe the process that stopped the bleeding. (b) Suggest why the area became red and swollen.
items.answer: (a) Platelets trigger conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin; fibrin mesh traps red blood cells forming a clot. (b) Pathogens entered; more blood flows to the area and white blood cells move in to destroy pathogens.
items.markingKey: (a) platelets [1]; fibrinogen → fibrin [1]; mesh / clot [1] [3] (b) infection [1]; white blood cells / blood flow [1] [2]
